name: aditi
transcript: Interviewer: Hi Vikram, thanks for taking the time to chat. I'm a student researching road-safety problems. Do you mind if I take a few notes and record our call just for my own reference?   Vikram: Yeah, that's totally fine. Go ahead.Interviewer: Could you tell me a little about your usual travel—do you mostly travel by car, two-wheeler, public transport, or a mix?   Vikram: I mostly take my two-wheeler to the office during the week, but I drive my car on weekends if I'm running errands or going out with my family.Interviewer: When you or someone you know has a road accident or vehicle breakdown, what usually happens next? Have you personally experienced or witnessed a situation like this?   Vikram: Actually, yeah. A couple of months ago, my younger cousin had a bad skid on his bike late at night. The tire slipped on a wet patch, and he was pretty banged up.Interviewer: Can you walk me through what happened? In that situation, what was the most difficult part—getting medical help, sharing the location, contacting family, or something else?   Vikram: Honestly, it was sharing the location and the delay that followed. He dropped his phone when he fell, and the screen shattered. He was somewhat conscious but in shock. A passerby eventually stopped, but it took them almost 15 minutes to figure out exactly which highway stretch they were on to tell the ambulance dispatcher.Interviewer: How did people find out about the accident and arrange help? Who took responsibility?   Vikram: The bystander called the ambulance and then used my cousin's broken phone—thankfully the voice assistant still worked—to call his mom. But she panicked because the bystander couldn't explain the exact landmarks to her.Interviewer: Was there any delay, confusion, or difficulty getting help? What caused it?   Vikram: Total confusion. The ambulance went to the wrong side of the divider first because of the vague directions. By the time he got to the hospital, it had been over an hour.Interviewer: How often do you think this problem occurs in your own circle or community? What makes you say that?   Vikram: All the time, especially for two-wheelers at night. People just don't know their exact coordinates when they panic, and communicating that to a dispatcher is a mess.Interviewer: That makes a lot of sense. So, we are exploring an idea called TRATA. The concept is a vehicle-mounted emergency response system designed to solve critical response delays after a crash. It includes automatic crash detection using on-vehicle sensors to instantly identify a serious accident without manual intervention. It also does parallel help dispatch, coordinating immediate assistance by notifying both professional emergency services and nearby network drivers, like cabs, to render initial aid. Lastly, it sends intelligent family alerts, automatically broadcasting to designated family members with real-time live location tracking and hospital routing details. This is still under development, and we are trying to understand whether it would genuinely solve a problem.   Vikram: Okay, wow. That sounds interesting.Interviewer: If a device in a vehicle could detect a possible serious crash, identify its location, and send an alert through a connected phone, how useful would that be in a real situation? Why?   Vikram: That would have changed everything for my cousin. If the location was just sent automatically to the hospital and his mom, the ambulance wouldn't have wasted time on the wrong side of the highway, and my aunt wouldn't have been relying on a confused stranger for updates.Interviewer: What would concern you most about this system—for example, false alarms, privacy, reliability, phone connectivity, or cost?   Vikram: False alarms, definitely. Chennai has terrible potholes. If I hit a bad bump, is it going to call an ambulance and freak out my family? Also, what if I'm in a dead zone with no network?Interviewer: Would you trust an automatic alert system to contact emergency services or family on your behalf? What would it need to do before you trusted it?   Vikram: I’d want a grace period. Like, a 15-second window where it beeps loudly in the car or on my phone, and if I'm fine, I can press a button to cancel it before it dispatches anyone. Without that, I'd be paranoid.Interviewer: What would make you actually use, recommend, or pay for such a system—and what would stop you from doing so?   Vikram: I'd pay for it if it was fully integrated and I didn't have to charge it separately. If it drains my car battery, or if I have to remember to plug the device in every day, I'd probably get lazy and stop using it.Interviewer: Last question. If this system cost an upfront fee to install, plus a yearly subscription to keep the 24/7 emergency dispatch and family live-tracking active, how would you evaluate whether to keep paying that yearly fee?   Vikram: Hmm. If the yearly fee is less than my streaming subscriptions, I wouldn't even think about it. It’s peace of mind. But if they ask for like five or six thousand rupees a year, I might reconsider unless the app shows me it's doing regular diagnostic checks on my car to prove it's actively working.
